opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was work I did with Yoon Kim, and the honest answer is that we had some intuitions going in, but part of it was empirical surprise.

The word-level approach is the classic Hinton-style distillation. At every position you take the teacher's full distribution over the next word and train the student to match it, usually with a cross-entropy against those soft targets. That makes sense for classification. But in sequence generation there's a mismatch: at test time you don't care about matching every local distribution. You care about the output you get when you run beam search, or some approximate search, over the whole sequence.

Sequence-level distillation targets that directly. You run the teacher with beam search, take the sequence it actually produces, and train the student on those outputs as if they were the ground truth. So the student learns to imitate the teacher's *mode*, roughly, rather than the whole spread of local probability mass.

I think a few things make that work well.

First, the student is small and has limited capacity. If you ask it to match the full word-level distribution, it spends that capacity modeling lots of probability mass on continuations that never matter in practice. Matching the teacher's beam output concentrates learning on the region of output space the teacher actually goes to.

Second, the data itself gets simpler. Real translation data is noisy and multimodal. The same source sentence could be translated many valid ways, and the references jump between them. The teacher's beam outputs are much more consistent and deterministic, so the student sees a cleaner, lower-entropy target. One thing we noticed was that the student trained this way became very peaked. It put most of its mass on a single output, so much so that you could often drop beam search and just decode greedily with little loss. That was a nice practical win for deployment.

Third, it partly sidesteps exposure bias. The student trains on whole sequences produced by a decoding process instead of only teacher-forced local predictions, so what it learns is closer to what it does at inference time.

So the high-level way I'd put it is that word-level distillation matches the teacher's beliefs, and sequence-level distillation matches the teacher's behavior. For generation, behavior is what you actually want. In hindsight, I think that idea, simplifying the training distribution by learning from a model's outputs, foreshadowed a lot of what people now do with synthetic data and training small models on outputs from big ones.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts matching local word distributions with matching whole-sequence outputs, but does not explain that dependencies among generation decisions make the complete-sequence distribution difficult to approximate with word-level distributions.

r002.rationale: It says to train on complete sequences produced by the teacher’s beam search and describes the student as learning to imitate the teacher’s mode, a concentrated approximation of its sequence behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we worked on back around 2016, and I think the intuition is actually pretty simple once you see it, even though it surprised us a bit at the time.

The standard way people think about knowledge distillation, going back to Hinton and others, is word-level. You have your big teacher model, and at every position in the sequence it gives you a full distribution over the vocabulary. So instead of training the student on the one-hot target token, you train it to match that whole soft distribution. The argument is that there's "dark knowledge" in the distribution: the teacher knows that "car" and "automobile" are both plausible here, and you'd like the student to inherit that.

The problem is that in a sequence model, matching local distributions is not actually what you care about. At test time, you're going to run beam search or greedy decoding, and what matters is whether the student produces a good whole sequence. And the word-level distributions are conditioned on the gold prefix during training. So you're teaching the student to imitate the teacher's uncertainty given a context the student will never see at test time, because the student generates its own prefix. That exposure bias issue is lurking in there.

Sequence-level distillation sidesteps that. You take the teacher, you run beam search on the training inputs, and you treat the teacher's output as the new target. Then you just train the student with ordinary maximum likelihood on that. So you're not approximating a distribution over the vocabulary at every step; you're approximating the mode of the teacher's distribution over entire sequences. In a sense it's a very crude approximation. You're replacing an exponentially large distribution with a single sample. But it's a sample from the right space.

And I think there are a couple of reasons it ends up working so well. One is that the teacher's outputs are just easier to learn than human translations. Human references are noisy, they have idiosyncratic choices, there's genuine ambiguity in how you'd phrase something. The teacher's output is more consistent, it's closer to what a model with this inductive bias naturally produces, so the student doesn't waste capacity trying to fit the noise. People later saw this really clearly with non-autoregressive translation, where distillation from an autoregressive teacher is almost essential, and the explanation is basically that it reduces the multimodality of the target distribution.

The second thing is that it's aligned with the decoding procedure. You're training the student to produce the sequence the teacher would have decoded, which is the thing you're actually going to evaluate. Word-level matching gets you something that's locally calibrated but doesn't necessarily translate to a good argmax after beam search.

And honestly, the third reason is practical. It's trivially simple. You don't need the teacher at training time anymore. You just run it once, generate a new dataset, and train normally. That was part of why we found it compelling: it's not a fancy loss function, it's a data transformation. We did also find that combining it with word-level distillation helped a bit, and interpolating with the original references helped, so it's not that the local information is useless. It's just that the sequence-level signal is doing most of the work.

r001.rationale: The response explains that word-level matching uses gold prefixes the student will not see at test time, but it does not clearly say that dependencies among generation decisions make the teacher’s complete-sequence distribution difficult to approximate with word-level distributions.

r002.rationale: It describes using the teacher’s decoded output as a new target and calls this a crude approximation that replaces the full sequence distribution with a single sample for the student to learn.

astra-6.text:
I think the intuition is that the large model is doing two jobs. It’s figuring out what a good translation looks like, but it’s also modeling all the different ways you could translate a sentence. And that second job is quite hard for a small model. There might be several perfectly reasonable outputs, with different word orders and different choices of words.

If you try to match the teacher’s word-level distributions, you’re asking the student to preserve a lot of that uncertainty. With sequence-level distillation, you let the teacher search for a good complete output, and then you train the student on that. So the teacher has already made a consistent set of choices across the sentence. The student’s task becomes much simpler.

You’re giving up some of the richness of the original distribution, but that can be a useful tradeoff when your goal is to produce one good answer with a much smaller model.

r001.rationale: The response says a small model struggles to preserve uncertainty among valid translations and that a complete output makes consistent choices, but it does not clearly explain that dependencies among generation decisions make the teacher’s sequence distribution difficult to approximate with word-level distributions.

r002.rationale: It describes the teacher selecting a complete output for training the student and notes that this gives up some of the original distribution’s richness, conveying a learnable coarse approximation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it is that the teacher is simplifying the problem for the student. In translation, there are many perfectly reasonable ways to translate a sentence. If you try to match the teacher’s distribution word by word, you’re asking a smaller model to represent all those alternatives, and to make them fit together into coherent sequences.

With sequence-level distillation, you have the teacher produce a complete translation, typically using beam search, and train the student on that. So the teacher has already made a consistent set of choices. The student doesn’t have to model the full diversity of possible translations; it can focus its capacity on learning one good solution. That can make decoding much easier, too—you can often get good results with greedy decoding because some of the work that search was doing has effectively been moved into the training data.

r001.rationale: It says word-level matching makes it hard to fit alternative translations into coherent sequences, but does not clearly explain that dependencies among generation decisions make the teacher’s complete-sequence distribution difficult to approximate.

r002.rationale: It describes training the student on complete teacher-generated translations, which provide consistent choices and let the student imitate one solution instead of modeling the full diversity of translations.
